headline: AI agents struggle with credentials securely, new principles propose a vault solution
summary: AI agents often need to log in, but current methods risk exposing plaintext passwords. New design principles aim to create a secure credential boundary, ensuring models never directly handle secrets.
details: Working with AI agents reveals that credential management, not model quality, is the most challenging problem. Agents often require login access, leading to secrets being exposed in chat transcripts and model contexts, making them unscoped and practically irrevocable.

A core principle is that the AI model should never hold plaintext credentials. A strict security boundary must exist, with only a narrow, explicitly approved execution layer allowed to interact with the secret, preventing misuse.

User approval for credential use needs to be frictionless, ideally a single tap, to prevent users from reverting to insecure practices. Approvals should grant ongoing access until revoked, not silently expire.

Grants should be specific, either per-login or explicitly all-access per agent, with a simple, single-switch revocation process. An activity log should provide a clear audit trail, allowing owners to easily see who has access to what.

Connecting agents must be as simple as adding a contact, avoiding complex provisioning. Standard OAuth consent for agents within other apps, using custom connectors that handle request links and statuses without carrying secrets, is recommended.

The login process itself should be separated: a dedicated, sandboxed browser session handles the plaintext credential, while the agent interacts with a scrubbed, labeled view of the page. This approach avoids reliance on site-specific adapters.
The author invites feedback on these design principles, particularly regarding task scoping, how agents prove credential use for specific tasks, and effective audit formats for human review.

headline: Kremlin-linked hackers exploited patched iOS and Android flaws to target diplomats
summary: Researchers link a Kremlin-sponsored group to attacks exploiting already-patched iOS and Android vulnerabilities, targeting diplomatic individuals through compromised and impersonated websites. The attacks aimed to steal sensitive data like browser cookies and
details: A group of hackers, assessed with "moderate to high confidence" to be part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws. Their targets included diplomatic delegations and high-profile guests, often linked to the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device, delivering tailored payloads to steal browser cookies, Wi-Fi passwords, and full mobile device data.

Attackers impersonated sites like america250.org, using america250[.]holiday as a reverse proxy to inject malicious JavaScript. Another target was theowo[.]club, impersonating Raffles of London OWO, a luxury hotel near sensitive UK government institutions where Ukrainian President Zelenskyy reportedly stayed.

The hackers also delivered attacks through compromised legitimate websites, including a top Ukrainian gas production company, and a Ukrainian web analytics service used by thousands of sites. Sekoia's attribution to the Kremlin is based on target profiles and similarities to previous APT29 attacks.

The infection vectors included direct JavaScript injection, proxy domains, and supply-chain compromise. After profiling the device, attackers delivered one of three zero-click exploit chains, which work without any user interaction.

One known exploit chain was DarkSword, an iOS exploit kit previously used by commercial surveillance vendors. All vulnerabilities exploited were "n-days," meaning they had already been patched, making only outdated versions of iOS or Android susceptible to the attacks.
